name: Evacuation

origin.note: Czyzowicz et al. posed evacuation of $k$ robots from a disk through an unknown exit on its boundary at DISC 2014.

derived_from.relation: Evacuation is a form of search with an extra requirement: "optimality in evacuation is measured by the time it takes for the last robot to reach the exit, whereas in traditional search, optimality is measured by the time it takes the first robot to reach the exit" [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]. The introductory paper notes its similarity with the cow-path problem, and that evacuating uniform agents on a line "is as hard as the cow-path problem" [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating].

summary: Robots start at the centre of a disk (or a polygon) and must all leave through an exit at an unknown point of the boundary, as fast as possible.
statement: $k$ unit-speed robots start together at the centre of a unit disk (or at the centroid, or at a given point of the boundary, of a unit equilateral triangle or square). An exit lies at an unknown point of the boundary; a robot recognises it only on reaching it. **Time** is the worst case, over exit positions, of the time until the last robot reaches the exit (in priority evacuation, where one robot is the **queen**: until the queen does; in weighted evacuation of two robots, a weighted average of their arrival times; in search, until a non-faulty robot has reached the exit and every non-faulty robot knows where it is).

primer.intro: Two people stand in the middle of a dark round room of radius 1 and know there is one door somewhere along its edge, but not where; they can talk by walkie-talkie. In evacuation the people are **robots**, points that move at unit speed; the room is a unit **disk**, the points at distance at most 1 from its centre; its edge is the **boundary**, the circle of radius 1; and the door is the **exit**, a point of the boundary that a robot recognises only when it stands on it. $k$ robots start at the centre of the disk. The goal is to minimise, in the worst case over exit positions, the time until the **last** robot reaches the exit. In the basic version there are two robots with **wireless** communication: a robot that finds the exit tells the other instantly, wherever it is.

ideas.title: Go to the boundary together, then split
ideas.idea:
1. Both robots walk together from the centre to the same point $A$ of the boundary (time 1).
2. One walks clockwise along the boundary, the other counter-clockwise, at full speed.
3. The robot that finds the exit tells the other by wireless communication.
4. The other walks straight across the disk to the exit, along a **chord** (the straight segment between two points of the boundary).
ideas.analysis: If the exit is found after each robot has walked an **arc** (a piece of the boundary) of length $x$ (so $x \le \pi$), the robots are $2x$ apart along the boundary, and the chord between them has length $2\sin x$. The total time is $1 + x + 2\sin x$. Its derivative $1 + 2\cos x$ is zero at $x = 2\pi/3$, so the worst case is $1 + 2\pi/3 + \sqrt3 \approx 4.826$ [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. This is exactly optimal (next idea).
ideas.why_it_matters: Searching the boundary in opposite directions and cutting across on a chord is the template for almost every later disk evacuation algorithm.

ideas.title: Two unexplored points far apart
ideas.idea: Look at time $1 + 2\pi/3$. Each robot needed time 1 just to reach the boundary, so together they have walked at most $4\pi/3$ of the boundary, and at least $2\pi/3$ of the boundary (minus a tiny $\varepsilon$) is unexplored. [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating] show that then there are two unexplored points at arc distance about $2\pi/3$ (measured along the boundary), so the chord between them has length $\sqrt3$. The **adversary**, an opponent who watches the robots and chooses the exit position, waits until some robot first reaches one of these two points and places the exit at the other one.
ideas.analysis: That robot is then at least $\sqrt3$ away from the exit and must still get there, and this happens no earlier than time $1 + 2\pi/3$. So every algorithm needs at least $1 + 2\pi/3 + \sqrt3$ in the worst case, which matches the algorithm above [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating].
ideas.why_it_matters: Counting how much of the boundary can be explored by a given time, then hiding the exit at the far end of an unexplored chord, is the basic lower-bound tool for evacuation.

ideas.title: Without wireless communication: catch the other robot
ideas.idea:
If robots exchange information only when they meet (**face-to-face** communication):
1. Go to the boundary together and split in opposite directions, as before.
2. The robot that finds the exit cannot call; it walks along a chord to the point where the other robot will be, meets it,
3. and both walk back along a chord to the exit.
ideas.analysis: The robot that finds the exit must cover the distance to the other robot and back, so the cost is larger: about $5.74$ for this simple version [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Cleverer paths that leave the boundary and come back improved it to about $5.6234$ [Disser2019Second], while the best lower bound is $3 + \pi/6 + \sqrt3 \approx 5.255$ [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace]. This gap has been open since 2019.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows how much communication is worth, and it is one of the simplest-to-state geometric questions still open in the area.

glossary.definition: a point that moves at unit speed and recognises the exit only when it stands on it
the unit disk: the points at distance at most $1$ from its centre, where the robots start (results are stated for $R = 1$)
the circle of radius $1$ that bounds the disk (for polygons, the perimeter of the triangle or square)
the unknown point of the boundary that every robot (in priority evacuation, the queen) must reach
a connected piece of the boundary; the arc distance of two points is the length of the shorter arc between them
the straight segment between two points of the boundary; a chord across arc distance $x$ has length $2\sin(x/2)$
communication in which a message sent by a robot reaches every other robot instantly, wherever it is
communication in which robots exchange information only when they are at the same point
an opponent that knows the algorithm, watches the robots, and places the exit where the evacuation time is largest
in priority evacuation, the one robot whose arrival at the exit ends the task; the other $\sigma$ robots are servants

history: Evacuation was introduced to capture the tension between **spreading the robots** to find the exit fast and **keeping them close** so that the others can reach it quickly [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. The first results already separated wireless from face-to-face communication. The community then tightened the two-robot face-to-face constants [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace] [Brandt2017Collaboration] [Disser2019Second] and added faults [Czyzowicz2017Faulty], priority (one robot must leave) [Czyzowicz2018Priority], asymmetric communication [Georgiou2022Asymmetric], other domains [Chuangpishit2020Triangles] and several exits [Pattanayak2018TwoExits]. Beyond disks, triangles and squares, the question was asked on the line and on rays [Chrobak2015GroupSearch] [Brandt2020Rays], in regular polygons with priority [Georgiou2025Polygons], on known trees as a planning problem that is NP-hard to solve exactly [Devillez2021Tree], and in the plane for an unknown shoreline [Acharjee2019Shoreline] or an unknown convex region to escape [Wei2016Competitive].

measures.name: Evacuation time
measures.description: worst-case time until the last robot (or the queen) reaches the exit, or the weighted average or search time where the goal says so; unit disk, unit speed

axes.name: Domain

values.label: unspecified bounded domain
values.definition: A bounded convex domain; the robots start together at a given point of it, in its interior or on its boundary.

values.label: unit disk, start at the centre
values.definition: The unit disk; robots start at its centre; the exit is a point of the boundary circle.

values.label: unit equilateral triangle, start at the centroid
values.definition: The equilateral triangle of unit side; robots start at its centroid; the exit is a point of the boundary.

values.label: unit square, start at the centroid
values.definition: The unit square; robots start at its centroid; the exit is a point of the boundary.

values.label: triangle, start on the boundary
values.definition: A triangle (the equilateral triangle of unit side unless the setting names another family); the robots start together at a point of its boundary, either given (at distance $y$ from the nearest midpoint of a side) or chosen by the algorithm, as the setting says; the exit is a point of the boundary.

values.label: unit square, start on the boundary
values.definition: The unit square; the robots start together at a given point of its boundary, at distance $x \le 1/2$ from the nearest corner; the exit is a point of the boundary.

values.label: the infinite line
values.definition: The robots start at the origin of the real line; the exit is at an unknown point at distance at least $1$; the measure is the competitive ratio, the evacuation time divided by that distance.

values.label: $m$ rays from a junction (a star)
values.definition: $m \ge 2$ half-lines share an endpoint, the junction; the exit lies on one ray at distance at least $1$ from the start; the measure is the competitive ratio.

axes.origin: Czyzowicz et al. posed evacuation in the unit disk with the exit on its boundary [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating], which remains the standard domain. Evacuation on the line had been raised just before by Chrobak et al.: robots that communicate only when they meet need time $9d - o(d)$ to evacuate whatever their number, as much as a single robot in the cow-path problem [Chrobak2015GroupSearch]; Czyzowicz et al. cite this as showing that evacuating several uniform agents "is as hard as the cow-path problem" [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Polygons followed: equilateral triangles and squares, first with wireless robots [Czyzowicz2015Wireless] and then face-to-face [Chuangpishit2020Triangles]. Czyzowicz et al. let the robots start either at the centroid or at a point of the boundary, and the start changes the answer: from the boundary of a triangle three or more robots do no better than two, while from the centroid three robots beat two [Czyzowicz2015Wireless]. A start on the boundary is therefore a separate domain value. Brandt et al. studied $m$ concurrent rays, citing Hammar et al. that "a problem with paradigmatic status in this framework is searching on m concurrent rays" [Brandt2020Rays]. Evacuation from a general convex region appears in a separate line of online-strategy papers [Xu2013Groups] [Wei2014Convex].

axes.name: Number of robots
axes.origin: Czyzowicz et al. studied the exact optimal evacuation time for $k = 2$ and $k = 3$ robots in the disk, and the asymptotic behaviour as $k$ grows: $3 + 2\pi/k$ face-to-face and $3 + \pi/k$ wireless, up to lower-order terms [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Most later disk papers fix $k = 2$, and even there the face-to-face case is not closed after several improvements [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace] [Brandt2017Collaboration] [Disser2019Second]. Specific small team sizes also appear in priority evacuation with one or two servants [Czyzowicz2018GodSaveQueen] and with polygons, where triangles and squares were solved for $k = 2, 3, 4$ [Chuangpishit2020Triangles].

axes.name: Goal

values.label: every robot must reach the exit
values.definition: The task ends when the last robot reaches the exit.

values.label: priority: only the queen must reach the exit
values.definition: One designated robot (the queen) must reach the exit; the others (servants) only help; the task ends when the queen exits.

values.label: search-and-fetch: a treasure must be brought to the exit
values.definition: A treasure lies at an unknown point of the boundary, and the exit at a known arc distance $\alpha$ from it; the task ends when some robot has carried the treasure to the exit.

values.label: weighted: a weighted average of two arrival times
values.definition: Two robots, a light one and a heavy one of known weight $w \ge 1$, both must reach the exit and stay there; with arrival times $t_1$ (light) and $t_2$ (heavy), the cost is $(t_1 + w\,t_2)/(1+w)$.

values.label: search: the exit is found and known to every non-faulty robot
values.definition: The task ends as soon as a non-faulty robot has reached the exit and every non-faulty robot knows its position for certain; the robots need not go to the exit.

axes.origin: Search ends at the first arrival and evacuation at the last [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Czyzowicz et al. introduced *priority evacuation*, in which only a distinguished robot, the queen, must reach the exit while servants help. They motivate it by a robot that alone "has the capability to address an urgent need at the target, for example, performing an emergency procedure, or closing a breach in the perimeter" [Czyzowicz2018Priority]. Georgiou, Karakostas and Kranakis introduced *search-and-fetch* (treasure evacuation), where a robot must carry a treasure to the exit. It is motivated by search-and-rescue, where drones must "locate a victim (the treasure) and bring her to safety (the exit)" [Georgiou2019SearchFetch]. They note that "this is the first time an explicit ordering on the tasks to be performed is imposed on two moving robots" [Georgiou2019SearchFetch]. Georgiou and Lucier weighted the arrival times of two robots on the line, a light one and a heavy one, and obtained priority evacuation on the line as the limit of large weight [Georgiou2023WeightedLine]. With faulty robots, *search* (the exit is found by a non-faulty robot and known to all non-faulty robots) is the first stage of evacuation: Georgiou et al. solved it on the circle with crash faults and with one Byzantine robot [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle], and Behrouz et al. note that the evacuation time "is inherently greater than or equal to the time required to find the exit" [Behrouz2025Byzantine]. Linear search uses the same two goals.

axes.name: Exits

values.label: one exit
values.definition: One exit, at an unknown point of the boundary.

values.label: two exits at unknown positions
values.definition: Two exits at unknown points of the boundary; the task ends when every robot has reached one of them.

axes.origin: Evacuation was posed with a single unknown exit [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Czyzowicz et al. considered two robots on a circle with $k$ exits whose distribution is known, where the robots do not know their own position [Czyzowicz2016MultipleExits]. Pattanayak, Ramesh, Mandal and Schmid studied two robots starting at the centre of the disk with two exits at unknown points whose arc distance $\alpha$ is known. They worked in both communication models and introduced labelled exits [Pattanayak2018TwoExits]. More exits help the robots, but only if the algorithm can use what it knows about the exits' relative position.

variants.title: Two wireless robots, disk
variants.summary: Two wireless robots evacuate the unit disk in exactly $1+2\pi/3+\sqrt3 \approx 4.826$.

results.note: Introductory and current best.

variants.notes: With one robot that has crashed and must be carried out, see Chauffeuring. In the unit disk of an $\ell_p$ norm, two wireless robots evacuate optimally for every $p \ge 1$, in time $5$ for $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ and about $4.7544$ at best [Georgiou2023Lp]. If every robot must visit every one of $k$ treasures, $k = 1$ is this problem [Kaminski2026Circles], a preprint.

variants.title: Two face-to-face robots, disk
variants.summary: Face-to-face, two robots need between $\approx 5.255$ and $\approx 5.6234$; the gap has been open since 2019.

results.note: Forced meetings exchange no useful information; simpler algorithm.
A second detour through the interior.

time.note: $\approx 5.6234$ versus $\approx 5.255$: a constant gap of about 0.37.

open: Close the gap between $3+\pi/6+\sqrt3 \approx 5.255$ and $5.6234$ for two face-to-face robots.
variants.notes: The "second cut" of [Disser2019Second] is a second detour through the interior: an upper-bound technique. Measured in the average case over the exit position, the trade-off between average and worst-case time is mapped, and $1+\pi$ is conjectured to be the optimal average for any number of robots, even wireless [Chuangpishit2019Average] [Chuangpishit2020MultiObjective].

variants.summary: Three wireless robots: between $\approx 4.159$ and $4.22$.

results.note: Introductory and current best.

open: Find the optimal evacuation time for three wireless robots.

variants.title: Three face-to-face robots, disk
variants.summary: Three face-to-face robots: between $\approx 4.519$ and $3+2\pi/3 \approx 5.09$.

results.note: Introductory and current best.

variants.summary: With $k$ wireless robots the time approaches $3+\pi/k$.

results.note: Introductory and current best.

variants.title: Many face-to-face robots, disk
variants.summary: With $k$ face-to-face robots the time is $3+2\pi/k$ up to $O(k^{-2})$; the separation from wireless is a factor 2 in the second term.

results.note: Introductory and current best.

variants.title: Three wireless robots, one crash fault
variants.summary: If one of three wireless robots may crash, evacuation takes between $1+4\pi/3 \approx 5.188$ and $\approx 6.309$.

preconditions: three robots, at most one crash
every boundary point must be visited by two robots, so some robot explores an arc of length at least $4\pi/3$

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1; the best asymmetric-persistent algorithm, Lemma 3); time until the last non-faulty robot exits.

open: Tight bounds for disk evacuation with one crash-faulty robot among three.
variants.notes: The best symmetric-persistent algorithm, with all three robots exploring in the same direction, takes $1+4\pi/3+\sqrt3 \approx 6.921$ (Lemma 1) [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]. The survey [Czyzowicz2019GroupSearch] (Theorem 17) states a weaker crash lower bound of $\approx 5.082$; the SIROCCO paper proves $1+4\pi/3$. Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2017Faulty].

variants.title: Three wireless robots, one Byzantine
variants.summary: With one Byzantine robot among three: between $\approx 5.948$ and $\approx 6.921$.

preconditions: three robots, at most one Byzantine

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2).

variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]. For $k$ wireless robots of which one may be faulty, Leonardos, Pagourtzis and Papaioannou prove that symmetric-persistent algorithms (all robots go to the boundary and explore in the same direction until told of the exit) need time at least $1+4\pi/k+2\sin(\pi/2-\pi/k)$ (Theorem 1, proved with a crash-faulty robot), and give a symmetric-persistent algorithm with time at most $3+4\pi/k$ for one Byzantine robot (Theorem 3), which for $k=3$ is about $7.19$, above $6.921$; with two Byzantine robots the time is at most $3+6\pi/k$ for $k \ge 9$ (Theorem 4); they also give face-to-face upper bounds (Theorems 5–7) [Leonardos2023Symmetric]. Behrouz et al. give upper bounds for $f$ Byzantine robots among $k > 2f$ wireless robots (Theorem 1) and among $k$ face-to-face robots (Theorem 2), and no lower bounds [Behrouz2025Byzantine].

variants.title: Priority evacuation (queen and servants), disk
variants.summary: Only the queen must leave; $\sigma$ servants (the paper writes $n$; $k = \sigma+1$ robots) help her find the exit.

preconditions: all robots start at the centre of a unit disk
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 5 of [Czyzowicz2018Priority]; it exceeds $2+\pi/\sigma+2/\sigma^2$, the leading terms of its expansion in $1/\sigma$, which is the form stated in the abstract (e.g. $2.913$ against $2.910$ for $\sigma = 4$). The naive bound is $2+\pi/(\sigma+1)$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1). The exact times of the algorithm are computed numerically, e.g. $3.113$ for $\sigma = 4$ against the closed-form upper bound $3.301$.

time.note: For large $\sigma$ the gap between the closed-form bounds is about $(4\sqrt2-5)\pi/\sigma \approx 0.657\pi/\sigma$ [Czyzowicz2018Priority].

open: Close the gap for priority evacuation; for one servant the bounds differ by about 0.25 (a 2024 preprint, not yet in the bibliography).
variants.notes: For a queen and three servants the bounds are about $3.374$ and $3.202$ [Czyzowicz2018GodSaveQueen]. The authors conjecture their algorithm for $\sigma \ge 4$ servants is optimal [Czyzowicz2018Priority]. The lower bound was checked against the full text (arXiv version) of [Czyzowicz2018Priority]: Section 4 proves the exact expression and the abstract states its asymptotic form $2+\pi/\sigma+2/\sigma^2$, so the two agree.

variants.title: Two robots with asymmetric communication, disk
variants.summary: When one robot can only send and the other only receive, evacuation lies strictly between the wireless and face-to-face optima; $\pi+2$ suffices.

preconditions: strictly above the wireless optimum; no explicit value

results.note: Introductory and current best.

open: Give an explicit lower bound above $\approx 4.826$ for sender/receiver evacuation.

variants.title: Two face-to-face robots, equilateral triangle
variants.summary: From the centroid of a unit equilateral triangle: between $1+2/\sqrt3$ and $2.3367$.

preconditions: two robots, face-to-face, start at the centroid

results.note: For $k$ robots: $\sqrt3+3/k$ against $\sqrt3$.

variants.notes: Wireless evacuation of triangles and squares was introduced by [Czyzowicz2015Wireless].

variants.title: Two face-to-face robots, square
variants.summary: From the centroid of a unit square: between $3.118$ and $3.4645$.
variants.notes: The lower bound is $1+3\sqrt2/2 \approx 3.121$ in Theorem 4.1 (the abstract states 3.118). Three and four robots evacuate in about $3.178$ and $2.664$ [Chuangpishit2020Triangles].

variants.title: Two robots, two exits, face-to-face
variants.summary: With two exits at unknown positions and communication only on meeting, the optimal evacuation time is $(1+\pi/2)R \approx 2.57R$.

preconditions: two robots start at the centre

results.note: Introductory and current best; optimal.

variants.notes: Bounds from the full version, supplied by the catalogue owner (a co-author); the robots are oblivious.

variants.title: Two robots, two exits, wireless
variants.summary: With two exits and wireless communication, evacuation takes between $2R$ and $(1+\pi/3)R \approx 2.047R$.

preconditions: two robots start at the centre

results.note: Introductory and current best.

open: Close the gap between $2R$ and $(1+\pi/3)R$ for two wireless robots and two exits [Pattanayak2018TwoExits].
variants.notes: Bounds supplied by the catalogue owner (a co-author). When two wireless robots move only along a circle of unit length, know the arrangement of the exits but not their own position, and start at arc distance $L \le 1/2$, they evacuate through one exit optimally in $3/4+L/2$ (Theorem 1) [Czyzowicz2016MultipleExits].

variants.title: Disk, two wireless robots of different speeds
variants.summary: With speeds $1$ and $v \ge 1$, two wireless robots evacuate optimally for $v \ge 2.75$; for smaller $v$ the bounds are within a factor $1.22$.

results.note: Introductory and current best: optimal (Half-Chord) for $v \ge 2.75$; for $1 \le v < 2.75$ the best of three algorithms, within a factor $1.22$ of the lower bound.

time.note: Tight for $v \ge 2.75$; a constant factor below it.

open: Optimal evacuation for $1 < v < 2.75$, for more than two robots, and face-to-face [Lamprou2020Fast].
variants.notes: Checked against the full text (arXiv version).

variants.summary: A queen and one servant evacuate the queen in about $4.819$, strictly faster than evacuating both; the lower bound is about $4.568$.

preconditions: a linear-programming relaxation over polygon instances

results.note: Theorem 8; also the first lower bound, about $4.3896$ (Theorem 17).
Same algorithm, with the improved lower bound.

open: Close the gap between $4.568$ and $4.819$ [Georgiou2025WeightedDisk].

variants.title: Disk, priority evacuation, queen and two servants
variants.summary: A queen and two servants evacuate the queen in about $3.833$ against a lower bound of about $3.631$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 10).

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Disk, search-and-fetch, two wireless robots
variants.summary: Two wireless robots find a treasure on the boundary and bring it to an exit at known arc distance $\alpha$ in $1+\pi-\alpha+4\sin(\alpha/2)$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2.1).

open: Lower bounds that separate wireless from face-to-face search-and-fetch [Georgiou2019SearchFetch].
variants.notes: With one robot, treasure evacuation is solved optimally when only a lower bound $\alpha$ on the actual treasure–exit arc distance $\lambda$ is known: time $1+2\pi-\alpha+2\sin(\alpha/2)+2\sin(\lambda/2)$ (Theorem 2; the paper writes $l$ for $\lambda$); when the exact distance is known, the best algorithm is within a factor $1.019$ (additively $0.157$) of a lower bound (Theorems 7, 8) [Georgiou2021Treasure]. Checked against the full texts of [Georgiou2019SearchFetch] and [Georgiou2021Treasure].

variants.title: Disk, search-and-fetch, two face-to-face robots
variants.summary: Face-to-face, two robots fetch the treasure in $1+\pi-\alpha/2+3\sin(\alpha/2)$, against $1+\pi/3+4\sin(\alpha/2)$ for $\alpha \le 2\pi/3$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3.1).

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, any number of face-to-face robots
variants.summary: On the line, face-to-face robots evacuate with competitive ratio exactly 9: extra robots do not help.

preconditions: any number of robots of maximum speed at most 1
any number $k \ge 2$ of unit-speed robots that communicate only when they meet
the argument covers algorithms whose explored segment does not grow at rate exactly $1/3$; [Bampas2019Speeds] call it partial and complete it (Corollary 3.4)

results.note: Section 2.2: two robots that cannot communicate wait half the time (equivalently, search at speed $1/3$); the finder goes back, meets the other and both return to the exit, in time $9d$, "the same time as one robot". No lower bound is claimed for two robots.

Each robot runs the doubling strategy, the finder waiting at the exit, or two robots search in opposite directions at speed $1/3$ and the finder catches the other (Section 2.2); with the lower bound of Theorem 3 this shows that $9d$ is optimal for any number of robots.

variants.notes: For two face-to-face robots the energy of group search can be traded against time; with maximum speed $v$ and time at most $9d/v$ the energy is about $8.42588\,v^2 d$ (the paper writes $b$ for $v$; Theorem 16) [Czyzowicz2019Energy]. Checked against the full texts of [BaezaYates1995Parallel], [Chrobak2015GroupSearch] and [Bampas2019Speeds].

variants.title: Line, any number of wireless robots
variants.summary: With wireless communication, two or more robots evacuate the line with competitive ratio exactly 3.

preconditions: consider the first time any robot reaches $d$ or $-d$ and put the exit at the other point
any number of robots and any communication model

results.note: Section 2.2: with instantaneous communication, two robots search in opposite directions; "if both robots must reach the goal, the distance increases to $4D$ and the time to 3 units" (their $D$ is $d$ here). Stated without a lower bound.

Algorithm $B^*$ with $v = 1$ (Corollary 4.3): two robots move in opposite directions at unit speed, the finder calls the other, which needs $2d$ more. Further robots can move with one of the two (the catalogue's own observation, see notes). [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation] attribute the bound to [Chrobak2015GroupSearch], which treats only robots that communicate when they meet; it is stated earlier by [BaezaYates1995Parallel].

variants.notes: Checked against the full texts of [BaezaYates1995Parallel], [Bampas2019Speeds], [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation] and [Chrobak2015GroupSearch]. Own observation of this catalogue, not taken from a paper: with $k > 2$ robots, let the extra robots move together with one of the two robots that walk apart at unit speed. Whichever of the two finds the exit, at distance $d$ and time $d$, every robot is then within $2d$ of it and all arrive by time $3d$; so ratio 3 holds for every $k \ge 2$.

variants.title: Line, two face-to-face robots of different speeds
variants.summary: With speeds $1$ and $v \le 1$, two face-to-face robots evacuate the line optimally: ratio $(1+3v)/(1-v)$ for $v \le 1/3$ and $9v$ above.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3.11); both robots must reach the exit.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, two wireless robots of different speeds
variants.summary: With speeds $1$ and $v \le 1$, two wireless robots evacuate the line optimally, with a ratio that changes form at $v = \sqrt{17}-4$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 4.8).

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, a sender and a receiver
variants.summary: A robot that can only send and one that can only receive wirelessly evacuate the line with ratio exactly $3+2\sqrt2$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1).

open: Close the gaps for one sender and many receivers ($2+\sqrt5$ against $5$) and for many senders and one receiver ($3$ against about $5.681$) [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation].
variants.notes: If an extra vehicle (a bike) can carry a robot faster, sender/receiver evacuation on the line has piecewise bounds in the bike's speed [Jawhar2025Asymmetric]. Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation].

variants.title: Line, $2f+1$ wireless robots, $f$ crash faults
variants.statement: $k = 2f+1$ robots, of which up to $f$ may fail to report the exit; every non-faulty robot must reach it.
variants.summary: With a near majority of faulty robots, evacuation on the line takes ratio about $7.437$ for $(k,f) = (3,1)$, tending to $4+2\sqrt2$; the lower bounds come from search.

preconditions: inherited from search with crash faults

results.note: Introductory and current best for $(3,1)$; $7.254$ for $(5,2)$ and $(7,3)$, $7.147$ for $(9,4)$, tending to $4+2\sqrt2$ (Theorems 2.2, 3.1, 3.2).

time.note: Constant gap against the search lower bounds.

open: Tight bounds for evacuation with $k = 2f+1$ crash or Byzantine robots [Czyzowicz2021NearMajority].
variants.notes: When every attempt to turn fails with known probability $\beta < 1/2$ (the paper's $p$), two wireless robots achieve ratio $3+4\sqrt{\beta(1-\beta)}+\varepsilon$ [Georgiou2024Disoriented]. Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2021NearMajority].

variants.title: $m$ rays, $k = m$ wireless robots at the junction
variants.summary: With one wireless robot per ray, starting at the junction, the competitive ratio is exactly 3.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Observation 1): each robot explores its own ray.

open: Starting off the junction with $k = m$: close $2+\sqrt{7/3} \approx 3.528$ against $4$ [Brandt2020Rays].
Fewer robots than rays ($1 < k < m$): the bounds $3+2\lfloor (m-1)/k\rfloor$ and $1+2\tfrac{m-1}{k}(1+\tfrac{k}{m-1})^{1+(m-1)/k}$ differ [Brandt2020Rays].
variants.notes: Checked against the full text (conference version).

variants.title: Triangle, two wireless robots starting on the boundary
variants.summary: Two wireless robots starting on the boundary of a non-obtuse triangle evacuate in half the perimeter if they may choose their start, which is optimal.

preconditions: non-obtuse triangle with sides $a \ge b \ge c$
the algorithm chooses the starting edge and point

results.note: Equilateral unit triangle, start on the boundary at distance $y$ from the nearest midpoint of a side; tight (Theorem 1), and $k \ge 3$ robots starting there do no better (Theorem 3).
Non-obtuse triangles (Theorem 1); separate tight or near-tight bounds when the adversary chooses the edge or the point.

time.note: When the algorithm chooses the start.

open: Face-to-face evacuation of general triangles, and wireless evacuation of obtuse triangles [Georgiou2026Triangle].
variants.notes: With $k \ge 3$ robots starting at the same point of the boundary the bound $3/2+y$ is still tight (Theorem 3 of [Czyzowicz2015Wireless]); see the setting with any number of robots. Checked against the full texts of [Czyzowicz2015Wireless] and [Georgiou2026Triangle].

variants.title: Triangle, any number of face-to-face robots
variants.summary: $k$ face-to-face robots at the centroid of an equilateral unit triangle evacuate in at most $\sqrt3+3/k$, against $\sqrt3$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Observation 3.2); for $k = 3, 4, 5, 6$ about $2.089$, $1.982$, $1.876$, $1.826$.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, weighted evacuation of two wireless robots
variants.summary: When the heavy robot's arrival counts $w$ times the light one's, two wireless robots achieve exactly $1+\sqrt{2w/(1+w)}$, between $2$ and $1+\sqrt2$.
variants.statement: Two unit-speed robots start at the origin of the line; the exit is at unknown distance $d \ge 1$. Both know which robot is heavy and the weight $w \ge 1$. The cost is $(t_1 + w\,t_2)/((1+w)d)$ in the worst case, where $t_1, t_2$ are the times from which the light and the heavy robot stay at the exit.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorems 3.1, 3.2). Without the identities, robots walking apart at unit speed achieve $1+2w/(1+w)$ (Theorem 5.1).

open: Weighted evacuation with more than two robots [Georgiou2023WeightedLine].
variants.notes: For $w = 1$ the cost is the average arrival time, ratio $2$; as $w$ grows the ratio tends to $1+\sqrt2$, below the ratio $3$ of evacuating both robots. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, weighted evacuation of two face-to-face robots
variants.summary: Face-to-face, the weighted cost is at most between $6.60258$ and $6.82843$, decreasing in $w$, well below the ratio $9$ of evacuating both robots; no face-to-face lower bound is known.
variants.statement: As in the wireless setting, but the robots exchange information only when they meet.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 4.1; numerical parameters in Theorems 4.12–4.14): $4+2\sqrt2 \approx 6.82843$ at $w=1$, decreasing to $6.60258$ as $w$ grows. Oblivious to the identities: $(2w+4\sqrt{w(w+1)})/(w+1)+3$ with $w$ known, $4w/(w+1)+5$ with nothing known (Theorem 5.2).

time.note: Constant gap: only the wireless lower bound is known.

open: Lower bounds for weighted evacuation of two face-to-face robots on the line [Georgiou2023WeightedLine].
variants.notes: The robots meet at a sequence of points away from the origin; a missed meeting tells a robot the direction of the exit. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Line, priority evacuation, queen and one wireless servant
variants.summary: A queen and one wireless servant bring the queen to the exit with ratio at most $1+\sqrt2$, against $3$ for evacuating both; no lower bound is known.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 6.1, the weighted algorithm as $w \to \infty$); the servant also reaches the exit.

time.note: No lower bound beyond the trivial one.

open: A lower bound for priority evacuation of a queen and one wireless servant on the line.
variants.notes: Georgiou and Lucier call this the strict version (the servant must also reach the exit) and note that the problem had been studied only on the circle before. Checked against the full text of [Georgiou2023WeightedLine].

variants.title: Line, priority evacuation, queen and one face-to-face servant
variants.summary: Face-to-face, the queen reaches the exit with ratio at most $2+\sqrt5 \approx 4.236$, far below $9$; no lower bound is known.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 6.2): the queen walks one way at unit speed, the servant the other way at speed $\sqrt5-2$; a servant that finds the exit catches the queen and brings her back. If the servant must also reach the exit, $6.60258$ (Theorem 6.1).

open: A lower bound for priority evacuation of a queen and one face-to-face servant on the line.
variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Georgiou2023WeightedLine].

variants.title: Disk, $k$ wireless robots, $f$ Byzantine
variants.statement: $k$ wireless robots start at the centre of the unit disk; up to $f < k/2$ of them are Byzantine. Every non-faulty robot must reach the exit; messages carry the sender's identifier.
variants.summary: With $k$ wireless robots and one Byzantine robot evacuation takes at most $3+4\pi/k$; general $f < k/2$ has upper bounds only, and lower bounds come from search and from the fault-free case.

preconditions: Theorem 1: search bound with $f$ crash-faulty robots, hence with Byzantine ones
every point of the boundary must be visited by $f+1$ robots
evacuation takes at least as long as search
fault-free bound of $k$ wireless robots (setting with many wireless robots in the disk)

results.note: Theorem 3 (search algorithm of [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle] plus a diameter); $3+6\pi/k$ for $f=2$ when $k \ge 9$, plus a term $\delta(k) \le 0.5687$ when $k < 9$ (Theorem 4).
Theorem 1, for every $f < k/2$; $G_e$ and $H_e$ are the evacuation times of two groups of robots that settle disputed reports, defined in the theorem.

time.note: For $f=1$: $3+4\pi/k$ against $3+\pi/k$, an additive gap $3\pi/k$; for general $f$ the gap is not quantified.

open: Lower bounds for evacuation of $k$ robots with $f$ Byzantine faults from the disk [Behrouz2025Byzantine].
variants.notes: Symmetric-persistent algorithms (all robots go to the boundary and explore in the same direction until told of the exit) need at least $1+4\pi/k+2\sin(\pi/2-\pi/k)$ with one faulty robot (Theorem 1 of [Leonardos2023Symmetric]), so $3+4\pi/k$ is within $O(1/k^2)$ of the best such algorithm. With $k = 3$ see the setting with three robots, where $\approx 6.921$ is known [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]. Checked against the full texts of [Leonardos2023Symmetric], [Behrouz2025Byzantine] and [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle].

variants.title: Disk, $k$ face-to-face robots, $f$ Byzantine
variants.statement: $k$ robots start at the centre of the unit disk and exchange information only when they meet; up to $f$ of them are Byzantine. Every non-faulty robot must reach the exit.
variants.summary: Face-to-face with $f$ Byzantine robots: $3+4\pi/k+2\sin(\pi/k)$ for $f=1$, and a general upper bound; lower bounds come from search and the fault-free case.

preconditions: Theorem 1: search bound with $f$ crash-faulty robots, hence with Byzantine ones
every point of the boundary must be visited by $f+1$ robots
wireless search bound; it holds face-to-face and for evacuation
fault-free bound of $k$ face-to-face robots (setting with many face-to-face robots in the disk)

results.note: Theorem 6; $3+6\pi/k+2\sin(2\pi/k)$ for $f=2$ (Theorem 7).

Theorem 2, for every $f$ (their $k$ is $j$ here, the number of conflicting reports); equals the bounds of [Leonardos2023Symmetric] for $f = 1, 2$. Against the trivial algorithm (every robot walks the whole boundary, time $1+2\pi$): the trivial one is better when $f \ge 0.3842\,k$ (Lemma 6), Theorem 2 is better when $f \le \beta k$ with $\beta < (\pi-1)/(2\pi) \approx 0.34$ and $k$ large enough (Lemma 7).

open: Lower bounds for face-to-face evacuation of the disk with Byzantine robots [Behrouz2025Byzantine].
variants.notes: Checked against the full texts of [Leonardos2023Symmetric], [Behrouz2025Byzantine] and [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle].

variants.title: Disk, $k$ face-to-face robots, $f$ crash faults
variants.statement: $k$ robots start at the centre of the unit disk and exchange information only when they meet; up to $f < k$ of them may crash. Every non-faulty robot must reach the exit.
variants.summary: Face-to-face with $f$ crash faults, $k$ robots evacuate in at most $3+2\pi(f+1)/k$.

preconditions: Theorem 1: search bound with $f$ crash-faulty robots, hence with Byzantine ones
every point of the boundary must be visited by $f+1$ robots
wireless search bound; it holds face-to-face and for evacuation
fault-free bound of $k$ face-to-face robots (setting with many face-to-face robots in the disk)

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 5).

open: Tight bounds for face-to-face evacuation of the disk with crash faults.
variants.notes: Checked against the full texts of [Leonardos2023Symmetric] and [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle].

variants.title: Disk search, $k$ wireless robots, $f$ crash faults
variants.statement: $k \ge f+1$ wireless robots start at the centre of the unit disk; up to $f$ may crash. The task ends when a non-faulty robot has reached the exit and every non-faulty robot knows where it is.
variants.summary: Search of the disk boundary with $f$ crash faults takes exactly $1+2\pi(f+1)/k$: every point must be seen by $f+1$ robots.

preconditions: every point of the boundary must be visited by $f+1$ robots

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2): robot $i$ explores $f+1$ consecutive arcs of length $2\pi/k$ from the point $2\pi i/k$.

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Disk search, $k$ wireless robots, one Byzantine
variants.statement: $k \ge 2$ wireless robots start at the centre of the unit disk; one of them may be Byzantine (it may lie about the exit). Messages carry the sender's identifier. The task ends when a non-faulty robot has reached the exit and every non-faulty robot knows its position for certain.
variants.summary: With one Byzantine robot, search takes exactly $1+4\pi/k$, as with one crash fault.

preconditions: Corollary 1: the crash bound of Theorem 1 with $f=1$

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3, with separate analyses for $k = 3, 4$ in Lemma 1 and Section 4.2).

open: Search of the disk with $f \ge 2$ Byzantine robots: only the crash lower bound $1+2\pi(f+1)/k$ and evacuation upper bounds are known [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle] [Behrouz2025Byzantine].
variants.notes: With one Byzantine and $f-1$ crash-faulty robots, search takes at most $1+2\pi f/k+2\sin(2\pi/k)$ (Theorem 4). Checked against the full text of [Georgiou2023OptimalCircle].

variants.title: Triangle, two wireless robots at the centroid
variants.summary: Two wireless robots at the centroid of the unit equilateral triangle evacuate in exactly $3/2+\sqrt3/6 \approx 1.789$.

preconditions: Theorem 2 with the start at the centroid, at distance $\sqrt3/6$ from the midpoints of the sides

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2: from an interior point at distance $y$ from the nearest midpoint of a side, $3/2+y$ is tight).

variants.notes: Three robots at the centroid do better than two (Theorem 4). Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Triangle, any number of wireless robots at the centroid
variants.summary: $k$ wireless robots at the centroid evacuate in $1+\sqrt3/3+3/k$, and no number of robots beats $1+\sqrt3/3$, which 8 robots attain.

results.note: Theorem 5.

Theorem 5.2: $6+2\lceil 1/r-1\rceil$ robots of communication range $r < 1$ suffice, hence 8 wireless robots; they report that 6 suffice with range 1, citing an extended version of [Czyzowicz2015Wireless].

time.note: Exact for $k \ge 8$; for $3 \le k \le 7$ the optimum is not proved.

open: The optimal evacuation time of $k = 3, \dots, 7$ wireless robots from the centroid of the triangle.
variants.notes: For range-limited robots, $\Omega(1/r)$ robots are needed to reach $1+\sqrt3/3$ (Theorem 5.1 of [Bagheri2019Triangles]); their Table 1 gives about $1.667$ and $1.6105$ for three and four robots with range 1, citing the extended version. Checked against the full texts of [Czyzowicz2015Wireless] and [Bagheri2019Triangles].

variants.title: Triangle, any number of wireless robots starting on the boundary
variants.summary: From a point of the boundary at distance $y$ from the nearest midpoint of a side, any number $k \ge 2$ of wireless robots needs exactly $3/2+y$: extra robots do not help.

preconditions: unit equilateral triangle, given start on the boundary
the argument does not depend on the number of robots

results.note: Introductory and current best: two robots walk the boundary in opposite directions (Theorem 1); more robots do no better (Theorem 3).

variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Square, any number of wireless robots at the centre
variants.summary: $k$ wireless robots at the centre of the unit square evacuate in $3\sqrt2/2+4/k$, against the lower bound $3\sqrt2/2$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 9): the robots split the boundary into $k$ pieces of length $4/k$ and the finder calls the others.

open: The optimal evacuation time of $k$ wireless robots from the centre of the square for fixed $k$.
variants.notes: Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Square, two wireless robots starting on the boundary
variants.summary: From a point of the boundary at distance $x$ from the nearest corner, two wireless robots need exactly $1+x+\sqrt{1+(1-2x)^2}$; the best start is $x = 1/2-1/\sqrt{12}$.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 6): the robots walk the boundary in opposite directions and the finder calls the other.

open: Optimal evacuation of the square by $k \ge 3$ wireless robots from a point of the boundary other than a corner.
variants.notes: From a corner, any number of robots needs $1+\sqrt2$, the two-robot time (Theorem 7); from the midpoint of a side three robots beat two (Theorem 8) [Czyzowicz2015Wireless]. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Disk, weighted evacuation of two wireless robots
variants.statement: Two wireless robots with known identities start at the centre of the unit disk; the heavy robot's arrival time counts $w \ge 1$ times the light one's, and the cost is $(t_1+w\,t_2)/(1+w)$ in the worst case over exit positions.
variants.summary: For two wireless robots in the disk the weighted cost is exactly $1+\pi$ when $w = 1$; for larger $w$ it lies between $\max(1+\pi,\ 3.618+0.782\,w/(w+1))$ and $1+d+\tfrac{2w}{w+1}\sin d$, tending to priority evacuation as $w \to \infty$.

preconditions: the two robots together need time $1+\pi$ to search the whole boundary
Theorem 2 (arXiv numbering), about $3.618+0.782\,w/(w+1)$; above $1+\pi$ for large $w$
linear-programming relaxation over exits at the vertices of a regular 7-gon, computer-assisted (Lemmas 4, 8)

results.note: Introductory and current best (Lemmas 5, 6, arXiv numbering): the robots split the boundary in halves, $d = \arccos(-(w+1)/(2w))$, while $w \le 21.8861$; for larger $w$ the heavy robot leaves the boundary early (a detour, with $d$ the solution of a non-linear system), which as $w \to \infty$ is the priority algorithm of cost $\approx 4.81854$.

time.note: Tight ($1+\pi$) at $w=1$; a constant gap otherwise, up to $4.568$ against $4.819$ in the limit of priority evacuation.

open: Close the gap for weighted evacuation of two wireless robots in the disk when $w > 1$ [Georgiou2025WeightedDisk].
variants.notes: The paper writes the cost as $w'x + y$ with $w' \in [0,1]$; its $w'$ is $1/w$ here. For $w \to \infty$ (their $w'=0$) the cost is priority evacuation, where the same framework gives the lower bound $\approx 4.56798$ (Theorem 1); see the setting of a queen and one servant in the disk. Checked against the full text (arXiv 2406.19490v1; theorem numbers may differ in the journal version).

further.note: Survey chapter (2019) on group search and evacuation: line search with crash and Byzantine faults, linear terrains, disk, triangle and square evacuation, faulty robots, several exits on a circle, and search-and-fetch. Read; it reports results of the papers placed in the settings.

Invited survey (SSS 2024) on how knowledge of the communication model, of faults and of the target's distance and speed changes the competitive ratio of linear group search and evacuation, with open problems. Read; no new results.
Time–energy trade-offs for evacuating two wireless robots from the line.

Two robots and one bike on the line: walking speed $1$, riding speed $v > 1$, one rider at a time; three algorithms in the wireless model and three face-to-face (Theorems 1–6), and a lower bound for both models (Theorem 8). Read.

One-page extended abstract (ICDCN 2020) summarising two-robot disk evacuation with two exits at known arc distance, labelled or unlabelled, wireless or face-to-face, and carrying a crashed robot to the exit at reduced speed; it states no bounds and defers to the full papers. Read.

Journal version of [Chuangpishit2019Average]: two face-to-face robots in the disk; families of algorithms minimising the average evacuation time over the exit position subject to a bound on the worst-case time, for every feasible bound (Theorems 6, 7); conjectures that $1+\pi$ is the optimal average. Read.

Evacuation of $k$ wireless robots from the centre of a unit square whose exit is at one of its corners, with crash faults that stop a robot, which a non-faulty robot must then carry to the exit at reduced speed; competitive ratios for $(k,f) = (2,1)$ (Theorem 1), $(3,1)$ and $(3,2)$ as functions of the slowdown. Read; neither the exit at a corner nor carrying is in the tree.
Evacuating rectilinear polygons; background from before the disk line of work.

Discrete evacuation of agents from distinct nodes of a known graph to known exits, at most one agent per node: an optimal offline strategy in polynomial time (Theorem 3.1); on trees, with communication at distance two, no $(2-\Theta(1/k))$-competitive online algorithm (Theorem 4.1) and an $O(1)$-competitive one (Theorem 4.2); NP-complete with agents restricted to subgraphs (Theorems 5.1, 5.2). A different sense of evacuation. Read.

Search for a point in the plane by $k$ robots of speeds $v_i$ with unit visibility, ending when the last reliable robot reaches the target: $\pi d^2/(2V) + o(d^2)$ with $V$ the sum of the speeds, asymptotically optimal (Theorem 1); asymptotically optimal bounds with $f$ crash faults (Theorem 2, Lemma 6); with $f$ Byzantine faults asymptotically optimal when wireless, and $(f+1)\pi d^2/(2k) + o(d^2)$ face-to-face for equal speeds and $k \ge 2f+1$ (Theorem 3). Read.

Search for a line (the shoreline) at known distance $d$ in the plane (they write $\delta$): every algorithm needs time at least $2d$ with three robots (Theorem 1) and $(1+\sqrt3+\pi/6)d \approx 3.2556d$ with two (Theorem 3), matching known upper bounds; the bound for three robots also holds for unknown $d$. Search, not evacuation. Read.

Groups of evacuees at one point of an unknown convex region of the plane, sharing information at all times, leave when all have reached the boundary: every strategy has ratio at least 3 (Theorem 1); $k \ge 3$ groups in equally spaced directions achieve $3/\cos(\pi/k)$ (Theorem 2); strategies on a grid network, ratio 3 with four groups (Theorem 6). Read.

One group, without communication with others, escaping an unknown convex region of the plane: a $19.64$-competitive strategy along growing semicircles (Theorem 1) and a $21$-competitive strategy on a grid network (Theorem 2). Read.

Escaping an unknown convex region once the boundary is known to all after the first evacuee reaches it: a 5-competitive strategy from one start (Theorem 2); from several starts, every strategy has ratio at least 3 (Theorem 1), and the strategy MES achieves 4 with two starts (Theorem 3) and $2+\sqrt5$ in general (Theorem 4), improving $4\sqrt2$ of [Liu2015Groups]. Read.
Groups that start at several points of an unknown convex region of the plane and share information: a $4\sqrt2$-competitive strategy for $n \ge 3$ groups (Theorem 1). Read.
Groups escaping a convex region. Title only.

Escaping an unknown convex region: a $19.64$-competitive strategy for one group (Theorem 1), a $14.37$-competitive strategy for two groups (Theorem 2), and $21$- and $17$-competitive strategies for one and two groups on a grid network (Theorems 3, 4). Read.

Related task: optimal average-case disk inspection.
Related task: two robots deliver a target to safety. Not read.
Plane search with agents of several speeds; a preprint, not read.
Search and rescue in the plane; a preprint, not read.

figure.caption: Evacuation from a disk: two robots start at the centre of a unit disk and must both reach an exit at an unknown point of the boundary. The animation runs the wireless algorithm of [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating] at unit speed: both walk to the boundary together, then search it in opposite directions; the one that finds the exit tells the other by wireless communication, and the other walks straight across the disk along the chord. With the exit placed at arc distance $2\pi/3$ (the worst case) the time is $1 + 2\pi/3 + \sqrt3 \approx 4.83$.

frames.label: Start: both robots at the centre O
Time 1: at the boundary together; they split
Robot 1 finds the exit, tells robot 2
Final: robot 2 arrives by the chord at 1 + 2π/3 + √3
